statement: Mu and posterior alpha share the alpha band and are told apart by topography and reactivity; the amplitude of the classical alpha rhythm tends to be larger than that of mu rhythms (both mostly below 50 µV), and mu is found with scalp EEG by eye in only a minority of adults (2.9% to 14% in the visually read EEG of the 1950s), in about half to 60% by spectral or coherence analysis, and in most if not all healthy adults by independent component analysis, though all healthy adults presumably have it. The site’s sections 7 to 9 run the mu rhythm at the strength of section 5’s alpha rhythm, an upper bound.
sources: Kane N, Acharya J, Beniczky S, Caboclo L, Finnigan S, Kaplan PW, Shibasaki H, Pressler R, van Putten MJAM (2017). A revised glossary of terms most commonly used by clinical electroencephalographers and updated proposal for the report format of the EEG findings. Revision 2017. Clinical Neurophysiology Practice 2:170–185. doi:10.1016/j.cnp.2017.07.002
Pineda JA (2005). The functional significance of mu rhythms: translating “seeing” and “hearing” into “doing”. Brain Research Reviews 50(1):57–68. doi:10.1016/j.brainresrev.2005.04.005
Niedermeyer E (1997). Alpha rhythms as physiological and abnormal phenomena. International Journal of Psychophysiology 26(1–3):31–49. doi:10.1016/s0167-8760(97)00754-x
Hobson HM, Bishop DVM (2017). The interpretation of mu suppression as an index of mirror neuron activity: past, present and future. Royal Society Open Science 4(3):160662. doi:10.1098/rsos.160662
note_for_auditor: Several numbers come from different sources: the 2.9% to 14% (visual reading, 1950s), the half to 60% (spectral/coherence analysis) and “most if not all” (independent component analysis) figures and the amplitude comparison. Check each against the source that holds it. The last sentence (how the site uses the figures) is the site’s own.

statement: The scalp signals a person can produce at will without an external stimulus are the sensorimotor mu (8–12 Hz) and beta (18–26 Hz) rhythms, learned in 3–10 hours of training and used for two-dimensional cursor control from electrodes C3 and C4 over the left and right sensorimotor cortex, slow cortical potentials, and posterior alpha raised by closing the eyes, which serves as an on/off switch that most adults can operate without training; P300 and flicker responses need a stimulus.
sources: Wolpaw JR, Birbaumer N, McFarland DJ, Pfurtscheller G, Vaughan TM (2002). Brain–computer interfaces for communication and control. Clinical Neurophysiology 113(6):767–791. doi:10.1016/S1388-2457(02)00057-3

Wolpaw JR, McFarland DJ (2004). Control of a two-dimensional movement signal by a noninvasive brain–computer interface in humans. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA 101(51):17849–17854. doi:10.1073/pnas.0403504101

Kirkup L, Searle A, Craig A, McIsaac P, Moses P (1997). EEG-based system for rapid on-off switching without prior learning. Medical & Biological Engineering & Computing 35(5):504–509. doi:10.1007/bf02525531

statement: Travelling waves have not been shown to be a control signal a person can produce at will. In motor cortex, beta waves recorded with a 100-electrode array in a tetraplegic person propagated at 15–35 cm/s, information about the reach target is encoded in evoked waves in monkeys, and wave-based decoding has been proposed but not demonstrated; the only operant control of cortical waves found is in mice (a preprint). Such waves at about 20 Hz are roughly 0.75–1.75 cm long, an order of magnitude below the 10–12 cm over which the skull blurs scalp electrodes together, so scalp EEG cannot resolve them; the waves EEG does see are the macroscopic 1–10 m/s kind, whose direction changes with the eyes open or closed, and distortion by the head makes waves seen only in EEG hard to interpret.
sources: Takahashi K, Saleh M, Penn RD, Hatsopoulos NG (2011). Propagating waves in human motor cortex. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 5:40. doi:10.3389/fnhum.2011.00040
Rubino D, Robbins KA, Hatsopoulos NG (2006). Propagating waves mediate information transfer in the motor cortex. Nature Neuroscience 9(12):1549–1557. doi:10.1038/nn1802

Takahashi K, Kim S, Coleman TP, Brown KA, Suminski AJ, Best MD, Hatsopoulos NG (2015). Large-scale spatiotemporal spike patterning consistent with wave propagation in motor cortex. Nature Communications 6:7169. doi:10.1038/ncomms8169
Dogadov A, Shulz DE, Ego-Stengel V, Ferezou I, Estebanez L (2024). Goal-directed shaping of cortical waves (preprint, not peer reviewed). bioRxiv. doi:10.1101/2024.09.10.612344
Muller L, Chavane F, Reynolds J, Sejnowski TJ (2018). Cortical travelling waves: mechanisms and computational principles. Nature Reviews Neuroscience 19(5):255–268. doi:10.1038/nrn.2018.20
Alamia A, VanRullen R (2019). Alpha oscillations and traveling waves: signatures of predictive coding?. PLoS Biology 17(10):e3000487. doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.3000487
Srinivasan R, Nunez PL, Silberstein RB (1998). Spatial filtering and neocortical dynamics: estimates of EEG coherence. IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering 45(7):814–826. doi:10.1109/10.686789
note_for_auditor: A mixed claim: a negative finding (no demonstrated volitional control of travelling waves in humans), speeds and wavelengths, and the EEG blur. Check each source for what is attributed to it; the wavelength arithmetic is the site’s own (speed over frequency). Say whether a human demonstration of travelling-wave control exists in the literature you can find; if it does, the claim must change.

statement: Mean change of mu-band power during cued motor imagery at the three central electrodes, from nine subjects, each in their most reactive band and relative to a 1 s rest reference (per cent; ± the standard deviation across subjects): left hand C3 −64.6 ± 25.2, Cz −56.8 ± 14.7, C4 −86.7 ± 9.4; right hand C3 −84.7 ± 16.8, Cz −58.3 ± 18.4, C4 −71.6 ± 18.8; foot C3 +89.3 ± 116.8, Cz −21.3 ± 65.1, C4 +112.7 ± 140.8; tongue C3 +145.2 ± 128.9, Cz +107.0 ± 66.8, C4 +133.6 ± 160.5. The authors note that C3 and C4 overlie approximately the hand representation areas.
sources: Pfurtscheller G, Brunner C, Schlögl A, Lopes da Silva FH (2006). Mu rhythm (de)synchronization and EEG single-trial classification of different motor imagery tasks. NeuroImage 31(1):153–159. doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2005.12.003
note_for_auditor: Table 1 of Pfurtscheller et al. 2006 (Neuroimage 31:153–159): check every mean and standard deviation against the table, the number of subjects, the electrodes, the band definition (each subject’s most reactive band?) and that the values are trial-averaged ERD/ERS percentages relative to a reference period. The claim reproduces the full table.
